newsitem.title: INDIA: India allows inspection of chemical weapons.
newsitem.headline: India allows inspection of chemical weapons.

text.p: India on Thursday opened its chemical weapons to international inspection for the first time, saying the monitoring would not compromise its security or hurt its chemicals industry.

"Now that the convention has come into force which collectively aims to eliminate such weapons, India has declared without any reservation all such materials in stock, production and storage facilities which will be open to international expert inspection at any time," the Defence Ministry said.
In 1993, India became one of the original signatories of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC).
The pact requires all signatories to destroy their chemical weapons within 10 years and provide information about production and export of listed chemicals which could be used to make arms.
They must also open their chemicals complexes for both regular and short-notice inspections. Under the convention, a June 26 deadline was set for inventory disclosure.
India currently chairs the convention's executive council and has hailed the treaty as a model disarmament pact.

"Our declaration is a reaffirmation of our commitment to the CWC, which we consider a multilaterally negotiated, comprehensive and non-discriminatory disarmament agreement," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
New Delhi says it developed chemical weapons only for defensive purposes.

"Adequate safeguards are in place for giving primacy to our national security interests and for protection of the interests and rights of our chemical industry," the Defence Ministry said in a statement.
"Should a situation threatening our security arise, our response will not be found wanting and our compliance with the CWC will not in any way compromise the security of our country."

India's ratification of the convention last September fuelled speculation that the country, considered a threshold nuclear power, would rely more heavily on a potential nuclear deterrent after relinquishing its chemical arms.
India conducted its only nuclear test in 1974 -- a decade after neighbouring China's first test, which followed a brief border war between the world's two most populous nations in 1962.
Both India and neighbouring Pakistan, which have fought three wars since 1947, say they have no nuclear weapons but experts say either nation can swiftly assemble them.
China has already ratified the CWC. Pakistan has not.

"Russia and Pakistan have not yet completed ratification formalities," the Foreign Ministry spokesman said. "All countries, particularly those in our region, should complete the ratification proceedings at the earliest."
Neither India nor Pakistan has signed the 1970 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty or the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, negotiated in Geneva last year.
New Delhi says the pacts are discriminatory and do not oblige declared nuclear powers to disarm. Pakistan says it will not sign them until India does.

Talks over a global ban on nuclear bomb-making material have been deadlocked all year in Geneva, where the two countries have led non-aligned nations in demanding the ban be linked to nuclear disarmament within a specified time frame.
